title: Object Detection
description: Going beyond a single label: bounding boxes, IoU, the two-stage vs. one-stage design split, and YOLO's real-time, single-pass detection approach.

lessons.title: From Classification to Detection: What's Different
lessons.description: Understand how object detection is a fundamentally different (and harder) task than classification.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how object detection differs from image classification in both output and difficulty.

sections.title: 🖼️ Classification: one label per image
sections.content: Image classification (covered in module 1) answers: "what is the single main subject of this image?" — producing one label (or one probability distribution over labels) for the whole image.

sections.title: 📦 Detection: multiple objects, with locations
sections.content:
**Object detection** answers a much richer question: "what objects are in this image, and *where* is each one?" The output isn't a single label — it's a *list* of detected objects, each with both a category label and a **bounding box** describing its location.

```
Detection output for one image:
[
  {"label": "dog", "box": [50, 30, 200, 180], "confidence": 0.94},
  {"label": "person", "box": [180, 20, 350, 400], "confidence": 0.89},
]
```

A single image might contain zero, one, or many objects — detection has to handle all of these cases, unlike classification's fixed "exactly one label per image" output.

sections.title: 🤔 Why this is a genuinely harder problem
sections.content: Detection has to solve two problems simultaneously: **what** is in the image (classification) and **where** each object is (localization) — for a variable, unknown number of objects. This means the model can't just output a fixed-size prediction the way a classifier does; it needs an architecture specifically designed to propose and evaluate many possible object locations across the image.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Confusing detection with classification.** They build on the same CNN foundations, but detection is a structurally different task requiring a different kind of output and architecture.

**Assuming an image always contains exactly one object to detect.** Real-world images often contain multiple objects, overlapping objects, or sometimes none at all — detection systems need to handle all of these gracefully.

**Underestimating the added complexity of predicting locations, not just labels.** Getting both the category *and* an accurate bounding box right, for a variable number of objects, is meaningfully harder than single-label classification.

questions.question: What is the key difference between image classification and object detection?
options: They are actually the same task with different names
Classification produces one label for the whole image; detection produces a list of individual objects, each with a label and a location (bounding box)
Detection can only be used on grayscale images
Classification requires more training data than detection
questions.explanation: Classification answers 'what is this image mainly of' with a single label, while detection answers 'what objects are present and where is each one,' producing a variable-length list of labeled, located objects.

questions.question: Why does object detection need to handle a variable number of objects per image?
options: Every image always contains exactly one object
Real-world images can contain zero, one, or many objects, and detection needs an output structure that can represent all of these cases, unlike classification's fixed single-label output
Object detection is only used on images guaranteed to contain exactly 5 objects
Variable object counts are not actually a real consideration
questions.explanation: Unlike classification's single fixed-size prediction, detection's output naturally varies in length depending on how many objects are actually present in a given image — the architecture needs to accommodate this.

questions.question: What two problems does object detection need to solve simultaneously?
options: Resizing and normalizing the image
What objects are present (classification) and where each one is located (localization)
Choosing a learning rate and a batch size
Converting the image to grayscale and back to color
questions.explanation: Detection combines classification (identifying what an object is) with localization (determining where it is, via a bounding box) — solving both together, for a variable number of objects, is what makes detection a meaningfully harder task than classification alone.

questions.question: What does the output of an object detection model typically look like, compared to a classifier's output?
options: A single label for the whole image, just like classification
A list of detected objects, each with a category label and a bounding box
A single numeric score with no further detail
An entirely new generated image
questions.explanation: Unlike classification's single label per image, detection produces a variable-length list of objects, each with its own label and location (bounding box).

questions.question: How many objects can a single image contain, according to the lesson?
options: Exactly one, always
Zero, one, or many — detection has to handle all of these cases
Exactly two, always
Detection only works on images with no objects
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly notes that a single image might contain zero, one, or many objects, and detection systems must handle all of these cases gracefully.

questions.question: What two problems does object detection need to solve at the same time?
options: Resizing and normalizing the image
What is in the image (classification) and where each object is (localization)
Choosing a batch size and a learning rate
Converting the image to grayscale and back
questions.explanation: Detection combines classification (identifying object categories) with localization (determining where each object is), solved simultaneously for a variable number of objects.

questions.question: Why can't a detection model just output a fixed-size prediction the way a classifier does?
options: Fixed-size predictions are always used for detection too
The number of objects in an image varies, so detection needs an architecture that can propose and evaluate many possible object locations
Detection models never produce any numeric output
Classifiers also use a variable-size output
questions.explanation: Since the number of objects varies from image to image, detection requires an architecture capable of proposing and evaluating a variable number of candidate object locations, unlike a classifier's fixed-size output.

questions.question: Why is object detection described as building on the same CNN foundations as classification, while still being structurally different?
options: Detection uses an entirely unrelated technology with no shared foundation
Both rely on CNN-based feature extraction, but detection requires a different kind of output and architecture to handle locations and variable object counts
Classification and detection are exactly the same task with different names
Detection cannot use convolutional layers at all
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that detection builds on the same CNN foundations as classification but requires a structurally different architecture and output format to handle object locations and variable counts.

lessons.title: Bounding Boxes and IoU
lessons.description: Learn how object locations are represented and how detection accuracy is actually measured.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe how bounding boxes are represented and compute Intersection over Union (IoU) conceptually.

sections.title: 📦 Representing a bounding box
sections.content:
A **bounding box** is typically represented by four numbers describing a rectangle around an object — commonly either (x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max) — the top-left and bottom-right corners — or (x_center, y_center, width, height) — the center point plus dimensions. Different detection systems and libraries use different conventions, so it's worth checking which one you're working with.

```python
# Corner format
box = {"x_min": 50, "y_min": 30, "x_max": 200, "y_max": 180}

# Center format (equivalent box, different representation)
box = {"x_center": 125, "y_center": 105, "width": 150, "height": 150}
```

sections.title: 📐 IoU: measuring how well two boxes overlap
sections.content:
**Intersection over Union (IoU)** measures how well a predicted bounding box overlaps with the true (ground truth) bounding box — the standard way to judge whether a detection's *location* is accurate, not just whether its label is correct.

```
IoU = (area of overlap between the two boxes) / (area of their combined union)
```

```python
def compute_iou(box1, box2):
    x_left = max(box1["x_min"], box2["x_min"])
    y_top = max(box1["y_min"], box2["y_min"])
    x_right = min(box1["x_max"], box2["x_max"])
    y_bottom = min(box1["y_max"], box2["y_max"])

    if x_right < x_left or y_bottom < y_top:
        return 0.0  # no overlap at all

    intersection = (x_right - x_left) * (y_bottom - y_top)
    area1 = (box1["x_max"] - box1["x_min"]) * (box1["y_max"] - box1["y_min"])
    area2 = (box2["x_max"] - box2["x_min"]) * (box2["y_max"] - box2["y_min"])
    union = area1 + area2 - intersection

    return intersection / union
```

• IoU = 1.0 means a perfect match (identical boxes)
• IoU = 0.0 means no overlap at all
• A common threshold (like IoU ≥ 0.5) is used to decide whether a predicted box "counts" as correctly locating the object

sections.title: 🎯 Why IoU is central to detection evaluation
sections.content: A detection is typically only counted as "correct" if *both* its predicted label matches the true label *and* its IoU with the true bounding box exceeds some threshold (commonly 0.5). This two-part correctness requirement (right label AND well-located box) is exactly why detection evaluation is more involved than plain classification accuracy — it's covered in more depth in the metrics lesson later this module.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Confusing the two common bounding box formats.** Mixing up (x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max) with (x_center, y_center, width, height) is a frequent source of bugs — always check which convention a library or dataset expects.

**Assuming any overlap counts as a correct detection.** A prediction with only a small sliver of overlap (very low IoU) shouldn't be counted as accurately locating the object — a proper IoU threshold is needed.

**Forgetting that IoU alone doesn't account for the predicted label.** A perfectly located box with the wrong class label is still an incorrect detection — both location (IoU) and classification need to be right.

questions.question: What does Intersection over Union (IoU) measure?
options: The total number of objects detected in an image
How well a predicted bounding box overlaps with the true (ground truth) bounding box
The confidence score of a detection
The size of the image in pixels
questions.explanation: IoU is computed as the overlapping area between two boxes divided by their combined (union) area, giving a standard way to measure how accurately a predicted box's location matches the true box.

questions.question: What does an IoU value of 1.0 indicate?
options: The two boxes have no overlap at all
The predicted box perfectly matches the ground truth box
The detection has the wrong label
The image contains no objects
questions.explanation: An IoU of 1.0 means the intersection and union areas are identical, which happens only when the two boxes are exactly the same — a perfect location match.

questions.question: For a detection to typically be counted as 'correct' in evaluation, what two conditions usually both need to be met?
options: The image must be grayscale and the box must be square
The predicted label must match the true label, and the IoU between predicted and true boxes must exceed some threshold (like 0.5)
The box must be centered exactly in the image
The detection must have exactly 100% confidence
questions.explanation: A detection is typically only counted as correct if it gets both parts right: correctly classifying what the object is, and locating it accurately enough (measured by IoU exceeding a threshold) — getting only one right isn't sufficient.

questions.question: What are the two common bounding box representation formats mentioned in the lesson?
options: RGB and BGR
(x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max) corner format and (x_center, y_center, width, height) center format
Grayscale and color format
JPEG and PNG format
questions.explanation: The lesson describes two common conventions for representing a bounding box: corner coordinates or center coordinates plus width and height.

questions.question: What does an IoU value of 0.0 indicate?
options: A perfect match between two boxes
No overlap at all between the two boxes
The boxes are identical in size but different colors
The detection has 100% confidence
questions.explanation: An IoU of 0.0 means there is no overlapping area between the two boxes at all, according to the IoU formula.

questions.question: What common IoU threshold is mentioned for deciding whether a predicted box 'counts' as correctly locating an object?
options: IoU ≥ 0.5
IoU ≥ 100
IoU ≥ -1
questions.explanation: The lesson mentions IoU ≥ 0.5 as a common threshold used to decide whether a predicted bounding box counts as correctly locating an object.

questions.question: Why isn't a perfectly located bounding box with the wrong class label counted as a correct detection?
options: Class labels don't actually matter for detection evaluation
A detection is typically only correct if both the label matches AND the IoU exceeds the threshold — location alone isn't sufficient
IoU already accounts for class label accuracy
Bounding boxes cannot have associated class labels
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly states both conditions (correct label and sufficient IoU) must be met — a well-located box with the wrong label still counts as an incorrect detection.

questions.question: What is intersection over union computed as, according to the formula in the lesson?
options: The sum of the two boxes' areas
The area of overlap between the two boxes divided by the area of their combined union
The difference between the box widths
The number of pixels in the smaller box
questions.explanation: IoU is defined as the overlapping area between the predicted and ground truth boxes divided by the total area covered by their union.

lessons.title: Two-Stage vs. One-Stage Detectors
lessons.description: Learn the two fundamental design philosophies behind modern object detection systems.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain the core difference between two-stage and one-stage detection approaches and their tradeoffs.

sections.title: 🎯 Two-stage detectors: propose, then classify
sections.content:
**Two-stage detectors** (like the R-CNN family) split the problem into two sequential steps:

1. **Region proposal** — first, identify a set of candidate regions in the image that might contain an object (without yet knowing what that object is)
2. **Classification and refinement** — for each candidate region, classify what object it contains (if any) and refine the exact bounding box

This two-step approach tends to be more accurate, since each stage can focus on doing its specific job well — but it's slower, since it involves running significant computation for potentially many candidate regions.

sections.title: ⚡ One-stage detectors: predict everything at once
sections.content:
**One-stage detectors** (like YOLO and SSD) skip the separate proposal step entirely, predicting object classes and bounding boxes directly and simultaneously across the whole image in a single pass.

This is significantly faster — often fast enough for real-time video applications — historically at some cost to accuracy compared to two-stage approaches, though modern one-stage detectors have substantially closed this gap over time.

sections.title: ⚖️ The core tradeoff: speed vs. accuracy
sections.content:
• **Two-stage** — generally higher accuracy, especially for small or overlapping objects; slower, better suited to offline or non-real-time processing
• **One-stage** — generally faster, often dramatically so; historically somewhat less accurate, though the gap has narrowed considerably with modern architectures; well suited to real-time applications like live video or robotics

This mirrors a familiar theme from the machine learning course: there's rarely a single "best" choice — the right one depends on your specific speed and accuracy requirements for the actual application.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming one-stage detectors are always meaningfully less accurate.** This was a bigger gap historically — modern one-stage architectures have narrowed it substantially, and are the standard practical choice for many applications today.

**Choosing a two-stage detector for a real-time application without checking whether it can actually run fast enough.** If genuine real-time performance (like live video analysis) is required, speed constraints often rule out slower two-stage approaches regardless of their accuracy advantage.

**Not considering the specific deployment constraints of the actual application.** As with backbone selection in module 1, the right detector architecture choice depends on real, concrete requirements — not just which one scores highest on a general benchmark.

questions.question: How do two-stage detectors approach the detection problem?
options: They predict everything in a single pass with no separate steps
They first propose candidate regions that might contain an object, then classify and refine each candidate region in a second step
They only work on images with exactly one object
They skip bounding box prediction entirely
questions.explanation: Two-stage detectors (like the R-CNN family) split the task into a region proposal step followed by a classification-and-refinement step, allowing each stage to specialize — generally at the cost of additional computation and speed.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of one-stage detectors like YOLO?
options: They are always more accurate than two-stage detectors
They predict classes and bounding boxes directly in a single pass, making them significantly faster — often fast enough for real-time applications
They require no training data
They can only detect one object per image
questions.explanation: By skipping the separate region proposal stage and predicting everything simultaneously, one-stage detectors achieve much faster inference, which is why they're the go-to choice for real-time applications like live video.

questions.question: Why might a real-time video application favor a one-stage detector over a two-stage one, even if the two-stage detector is somewhat more accurate?
options: Two-stage detectors cannot process video at all

Real-time applications have strict speed requirements that a slower two-stage detector may not be able to meet, making the faster one-stage approach more practical despite a potential accuracy tradeoff
One-stage detectors are always more accurate in every case
Speed has no actual bearing on which detector to choose
questions.explanation: When an application genuinely requires real-time performance, meeting that speed constraint often takes priority — a highly accurate but too-slow detector simply isn't usable for that use case, making a faster one-stage detector the more practical choice despite potentially somewhat lower accuracy.

questions.question: What is the first step in a two-stage detector's pipeline?
options: Directly predicting classes and boxes in a single pass
Region proposal — identifying candidate regions that might contain an object
Non-Maximum Suppression
Converting the image to grayscale
questions.explanation: Two-stage detectors first perform region proposal, identifying candidate regions that might contain objects, before classifying and refining them in a second step.

questions.question: What historically was the main tradeoff of one-stage detectors compared to two-stage detectors?
options: One-stage detectors were always more accurate with no downsides
One-stage detectors were significantly faster but historically somewhat less accurate, though the gap has narrowed
One-stage detectors could not process video at all
There was never any tradeoff between the two approaches
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that one-stage detectors traded some accuracy for a significant speed advantage historically, though modern one-stage detectors have substantially closed that gap.

questions.question: Which family of detectors does the lesson give as an example of the two-stage approach?
options: YOLO
The R-CNN family
SSD
ViT
questions.explanation: The R-CNN family is given as the example of two-stage detectors, which use a region proposal step followed by classification and refinement.

questions.question: Why might a two-stage detector be preferred for offline processing of images with small or overlapping objects?
options: Two-stage detectors cannot process small objects at all
Two-stage detectors generally achieve higher accuracy, especially for small or overlapping objects, at the cost of speed, which is acceptable for non-real-time processing
Offline processing requires the fastest possible detector regardless of accuracy
Two-stage detectors are always faster than one-stage detectors
questions.explanation: Since two-stage detectors tend to be more accurate especially for challenging cases like small or overlapping objects, and offline processing doesn't have strict real-time speed constraints, the accuracy advantage can be worth the added computation.

questions.question: What does the lesson say determines the 'right' detector architecture choice for an application?
options: Always choosing whichever detector scores highest on a general benchmark
The specific speed and accuracy requirements of the actual application
The detector's publication date
The number of letters in the detector's name
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that the right detector choice depends on the actual application's specific speed and accuracy requirements, not a one-size-fits-all answer or benchmark ranking alone.

lessons.title: YOLO: Real-Time Object Detection
lessons.description: Get an intuitive understanding of the influential one-stage detector that made real-time detection practical.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain the core intuition behind how YOLO detects objects in a single pass.

sections.title: 👀 YOLO: You Only Look Once
sections.content: **YOLO** gets its name from its central idea: rather than scanning the image piece by piece or running a separate region-proposal step, it looks at the entire image *once*, dividing it into a grid, and has each grid cell directly predict whether an object's center falls there, along with that object's bounding box and class — all in a single forward pass through the network.

sections.title: 🎲 The grid-based prediction idea
sections.content:
```
Image divided into a grid, e.g. 7x7 cells:
[ .  .  .  .  .  .  . ]
[ .  .  🐕 .  .  .  . ]   ← this cell predicts: "dog", with a box, if an object's center lands here
[ .  .  .  .  .  .  . ]
[ .  .  .  .  🧍 .  . ]   ← this cell predicts: "person"
[ .  .  .  .  .  .  . ]
```

Each grid cell predicts (a) whether it contains the center of an object, (b) that object's bounding box coordinates, and (c) what class it belongs to — all computed simultaneously across the whole grid in one pass, which is exactly why YOLO is so fast.

sections.title: 🧹 Cleaning up predictions: Non-Maximum Suppression
sections.content:
A single object often triggers multiple overlapping candidate detections from nearby grid cells. **Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)** cleans this up: it keeps only the highest-confidence detection among a group of heavily overlapping predictions (measured using IoU from the earlier lesson) and discards the redundant, lower-confidence overlapping ones.

```python
# Conceptual NMS process
# 1. Sort all candidate detections by confidence, highest first
# 2. Keep the highest-confidence detection
# 3. Remove any remaining candidates that overlap it heavily (high IoU)
# 4. Repeat with the next highest-confidence remaining detection
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming YOLO literally examines each grid cell in sequence, one at a time.** All predictions across the entire grid are computed together in a single forward pass — the "grid" is a way of structuring the output, not a step-by-step scanning process.

**Forgetting Non-Maximum Suppression is a necessary cleanup step.** Without it, a single real object would often be reported as several duplicate, overlapping detections.

**Assuming YOLO's grid-based approach struggles equally with all object sizes.** Different YOLO versions and variants have specifically evolved (with techniques beyond this lesson's scope) to better handle detecting both small and large objects within the same grid-based framework.

questions.question: What does YOLO's name ("You Only Look Once") reflect about its approach?
options: It can only be used on a single image ever
It predicts objects and their locations in a single forward pass through the network, rather than using a separate region-proposal step or scanning the image multiple times
It only detects exactly one object per image
It requires looking at the same image multiple times for accuracy
questions.explanation: YOLO processes the entire image in one single pass, directly predicting all object locations and classes at once — this single-pass efficiency is exactly what gives it its name and its speed advantage over two-stage approaches.

questions.question: What problem does Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) solve?
options: It speeds up the initial image loading process
It removes redundant, overlapping duplicate detections of the same object, keeping only the highest-confidence one
It converts the image to grayscale before detection
It resizes the image to the model's expected input size
questions.explanation: Since nearby grid cells can each trigger a detection for the same real object, NMS cleans up these overlapping duplicate predictions by keeping only the highest-confidence detection and discarding heavily overlapping (high IoU) redundant ones.

questions.question: What does each grid cell in YOLO's grid-based approach predict?
options: The entire image's overall classification label
Whether an object's center falls in that cell, along with that object's bounding box and class, if so
The exact pixel values of the whole image
Only whether the cell is empty or not, with no other information
questions.explanation: Each cell in YOLO's grid is responsible for predicting whether an object's center lands within it, and if so, that object's bounding box coordinates and class — all cells make these predictions simultaneously in a single pass.

questions.question: How many forward passes through the network does YOLO typically need to detect all objects in an image?
options: One single pass
One pass per object in the image
Multiple passes, once per grid cell
An unlimited number of passes
questions.explanation: YOLO's key innovation is predicting all objects and their locations in a single forward pass through the network, which is reflected in its name.

questions.question: What three things does each grid cell in YOLO predict?
options: The image's file format, resolution, and color depth
Whether an object's center falls there, that object's bounding box, and its class
The total number of objects in the entire image
The camera settings used to take the photo
questions.explanation: Each grid cell predicts whether an object's center is located there, along with that object's bounding box coordinates and class, computed simultaneously across the grid.

questions.question: What does Non-Maximum Suppression use to decide which overlapping detections to discard?
options: Random selection
IoU between overlapping candidate detections, keeping the highest-confidence one
The alphabetical order of the class labels
The file size of the image
questions.explanation: NMS uses IoU to identify heavily overlapping candidate detections and keeps only the highest-confidence one among them, discarding the rest as redundant.

questions.question: Why is it inaccurate to think of YOLO as scanning an image's grid cells one at a time in sequence?
options: YOLO doesn't actually use a grid at all
All predictions across the entire grid are computed together in a single forward pass — the grid structures the output, not a step-by-step scanning process
YOLO processes only a single grid cell per image
Grid cells are processed in a random order each time
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns against this misconception: the grid is a way of structuring simultaneous predictions across the whole image, not a sequential scan.

questions.question: Without Non-Maximum Suppression, what problem would likely occur with YOLO's raw predictions?
options: The model would fail to detect any objects at all
A single real object would often be reported as multiple duplicate, overlapping detections
The image would be resized incorrectly
The model would only work on grayscale images
questions.explanation: Since nearby grid cells often trigger overlapping detections for the same real object, NMS is necessary to clean up these duplicates — without it, a single object could be reported multiple times.
